subject: Climate & Environment
title: Hailstorms and Supercells
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Hailstorms and Supercells.

hook.text: The largest hailstone ever recorded was the size of a volleyball — 20 cm across.

buildup.text: Hail forms when powerful updrafts in supercells carry raindrops high enough to freeze.

discovery.text: Stones cycle up and down inside the storm, adding layers of ice until they're too heavy to float.

twist.text: A single hailstorm in 2022 caused $2.5 billion in damage in France in under an hour.

climax.text: Climate change may increase hail intensity. Warmer air holds more moisture for storms to use.

punchline.text: The sky can throw rocks. And they're getting bigger.

quiz.question: How does hail form inside a thunderstorm?
options: Updrafts carry raindrops high enough to freeze repeatedly
Rain freezes as it falls through cold air
Ice crystals form directly from water vapor

details.summary: Hailstorms form within powerful supercell thunderstorms where strong updrafts loft water droplets above the freezing level repeatedly, building layers of ice. Hailstones can exceed 15 centimeters in diameter and cause billions in damage to crops, vehicles, and buildings annually.
details.whyItMatters: Hail is the costliest severe weather hazard for agriculture and property. Understanding supercell dynamics helps predict which storms will produce damaging hail.
takeaways: Hail forms when strong updrafts keep ice aloft through multiple growth cycles
The largest recorded hailstone was 20 cm in diameter
Hail causes over 10 billion dollars in US damage per year on average

faq.question: How do hailstones grow so large?
faq.answer: Strong updrafts in supercells carry ice particles through the freezing zone repeatedly. Each pass adds a layer of ice, building the stone larger. Only when the stone becomes too heavy for the updraft to support does it fall to the ground.

faq.question: Is hail becoming more damaging due to climate change?
faq.answer: Evidence is mixed. Warmer air increases moisture and instability that fuel supercells, but also raises freezing levels, potentially reducing hail reaching the ground. Damage costs are rising mainly due to urbanization and more property at risk.
